title: Redwood edge cases demo - long context, high TPS, streaming/backpressure
summary: Redwood ran through an edge-case focused demo highlighting long-context handling, high TPS behavior, streaming backpressure and timeout behavior. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private and is most concerned about tail latency, timeouts under bursty TPS, and data residency/KMS. Agreed next steps: share pricing and private deployment checklist, run a POC benchmark with Atlas sample prompts/traffic, and follow up with security docs.
topics: API demo: long context support and KV cache
Optimize: batching, quantization recommendations, backpressure handling
High TPS load behaviour and autoscaling
action_items: Liam Patel: send pricing sheet + private deployment checklist by 2025-11-07
Sofia Martinez: schedule POC benchmark and request sample prompt set/traffic profile by 2025-11-12
Jordan Lee (Atlas): provide sample prompt set and 1-week traffic trace by 2025-11-06
Harper Nguyen: share initial optimization recommendations (batching/quantization) and runbook link by 2025-11-10
next_steps: Send security whitepaper and SOC2 summary
Run a 72-hour POC with dedicated pool for 5 GPUs simulating 2k TPS bursts
Demo private deployment checklist and networking diagram
Follow-up call to review benchmark results and sizing
meeting_header: Date: 2025-11-05 | Time: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Liam (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Harper (Redwood SE), Jordan (CTO - Atlas), Priya (Lead ML Eng), Ethan (SRE), Maya (Product)
transcript:
[00:00] Liam Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Liam, AE at Redwood, with Sofia and Harper from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Jordan Lee: Good thanks, ready to see the edge-case stuff. We've got a hard requirement around long contexts for our audit logs and very bursty TPS so hoping to see how Redwood handles that.
[00:18] Sofia Martinez: Great, we'll start with an API walkthrough for a long-context scenario, then show the Console routing and Optimize suggestions for high TPS and streaming backpressure.
[00:30] Priya Shah: Quick note, our main pain points: tail latency with 100k token-ish contexts, streaming cancellations when downstream backpressure hits, and predictable costing. Also SOC2 and KMS are must-haves.
[00:44] Harper Nguyen: Perfect. We'll surface how prefix/KV caching helps long contexts and how the runtime picks kernels, also how batching and quantization help cost at scale.
[00:57] Ethan Park: Also curious about timeouts — our current infra sees 503s when clients drop connections mid-stream, how does Redwood degrade?
[01:10] Sofia Martinez: We'll demo graceful fallback policies — for example automatic fallback to a lower-cost model variant or a cached response when latency exceeds SLO.
[01:19] Liam Patel: Ok jumping into the API. (screen share) Here's a sample request building a 150k token conversational context — note we chunk and stream KV keys.
[01:31] Sofia Martinez: (demoing) The API accepts context blobs, we maintain a KV cache per conversation to avoid re-encoding prefixes. In this case you see the latency for initial first-token is higher but subsequent requests with overlapping context drop to single-digit ms per token.
[01:46] Jordan Lee: Did you say 150k tokens? That sounds like a lot, our compliance logs can be that long. Any limits?
[01:53] Harper Nguyen: We support very long contexts via segmented KV caches; practical limits depend on model architecture and memory, but we have customers hitting 200k with special quantization and chunking. You'll want to pin a model variant and we can recommend quant profiles.
[02:07] Priya Shah: How do you maintain semantic consistency if you chunk? We can't have the model forget earlier context.
[02:14] Sofia Martinez: Good question. We use overlap-aware stitching — older segments are summarized into condensed KV entries, plus we can keep a gold prefix for critical tokens. There are tradeoffs and that's where Redwood Optimize flags prompts likely to lose signal.
[02:30] Jordan Lee: OK. Now high TPS — we regularly see occasional bursts to ~2k TPS for short windows — what's the behavior?
[02:39] Harper Nguyen: For bursts we recommend Dedicated with autoscale policies and burst capacity. Our load tests show sustained 2k TPS on a 8-GPU pool with continuous batching and intelligent routing, but the key is queue management and backpressure handling.
[02:53] Ethan Park: What happens to streaming clients when backpressure occurs — do you drop streams or buffer? We can't have 30s stalls.
[03:01] Sofia Martinez: We have a few strategies: 1) Client-side streaming with small chunked frames so clients can process partial outputs; 2) Server-side adaptive batching that prioritizes low-latency routes; 3) When GPU queues fill, we surface explicit backpressure signals in the API so clients can throttle or switch to non-streamed fallback.
[03:18] Liam Patel: (shows Console) Here you can configure route policies — route by latency SLO or cost and set automatic fallback to a smaller model or cached answer after X ms.
[03:33] Maya Ortiz: Nice, can that be per-tenant? We need different SLAs per product line.
[03:37] Harper Nguyen: Yes per-route and per-customer. You can also set canary rollouts and automatic rollback on error rate spikes.
[03:46] Priya Shah: What about timeouts? If our clients have a 10s front-end timeout, how do we avoid partial failure?
[03:54] Sofia Martinez: You can set consumer-level timeouts integrated with the SDK. We also provide hedging — duplicating requests to a cold replica — and a streaming TTL that will attempt to return a condensed summary if the full stream can't finish.
[04:07] Jordan Lee: How accurate is condensed summary? We need fidelity for audits.
[04:11] Harper Nguyen: For audit-critical content we recommend Dedicated or Private with more memory and no summarization, or store raw token streams into your secure S3 and let Redwood fetch them when needed. We also support end-to-end encryption via KMS.
[04:27] Ethan Park: Can you walk through a failure scenario? Like sudden spike, one GPU OOM, streams getting queued?
[04:34] Sofia Martinez: Sure. (diagram) If a GPU OOMs, runtime drains and reschedules shards, routing layer directs new requests to healthy variants, and autoscaler triggers new capacity based on queue length. For streams that are mid-flight, you get either graceful reconnect with a resume token or a fallback cached response depending on policy.
[04:52] Jordan Lee: Resume token — does that mean the client can reattach and continue?
[04:56] Harper Nguyen: Yes, we emit a resumable stream token that captures the last KV pointer; clients can reconnect and continue from that point if the model variant is compatible. There are edge cases with quantized model variants that can change tokenization slightly — we'll flag compatibility in the Console.
[05:14] Priya Shah: About quantization — will 4-bit/8-bit quantization affect our auditing accuracy?
[05:20] Sofia Martinez: Quantization can affect subtle generation details; Redwood Optimize runs a quality regression against your eval prompts and gives a quality delta. We only recommend quant profiles with acceptable deltas and show where they matter most.
[05:33] Jordan Lee: Security questions — we need SOC2, SSO, SAML, RBAC, KMS, and audit logs retained for seven years.
[05:41] Liam Patel: We are SOC2 Type II, support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and customer-managed KMS in Private deployments. For retention windows like seven years we integrate with your archival storage; we'll send the security whitepaper and compliance attestation.
[05:56] Maya Ortiz: In Private/on-prem, how big is the control plane footprint? We have air-gapped requirements.
[06:02] Harper Nguyen: We offer a private control plane and an on-prem bundle. Air-gapped installs are possible; lifecycle tools are available but upgrades require coordination. We'll include the network diagram in the checklist.
[06:12] Jordan Lee: Ok demo the streaming backpressure — show a simulated burst and what the client sees.
[06:18] Sofia Martinez: (simulated demo) Kicking off 2k TPS with variable payload sizes. You'll see some requests get queued, we mark backpressure on the route, the SDK receives a 429-backpressure header and adaptive retry recommended.
[06:33] Ethan Park: Does Redwood automatically throttle to maintain SLOs or does the client need to implement adaptive behavior?
[06:38] Harper Nguyen: We do both. The routing policy can enforce rate limits and shed load to keep latency SLO; the SDK exposes backpressure signals so clients can back off gracefully. We also have a server-side hedging policy to reduce tail latency.
[06:51] Priya Shah: Show us the logs and metrics — latency percentiles, queue depth, token-per-second counters.
[06:58] Sofia Martinez: (Console) Here are per-route dashboards: p50/p95/p99, queue length, GPU utilization, tokens/sec, and KV cache hit rate. In this simulated spike p99 goes up but we have automated fallback after 800ms.
[07:14] Jordan Lee: Can users see which model kernels are chosen? We tune to CUDA kernels often.
[07:18] Harper Nguyen: Yes we surface kernel selection and a recommended kernel profile for your workload. We also recommend sequence-length aware kernels for long contexts.
[07:28] Liam Patel: Quick note on pricing: long contexts and high TPS both increase token and GPU costs — Optimize will show a cost per 1M tokens with current config and then suggested changes.
[07:39] Jordan Lee: Can we set a hard cost cap? We need to avoid billing surprises.
[07:43] Sofia Martinez: Yes, we have quota and budget alerts and automatic throttles at spending thresholds.
[07:49] Maya Ortiz: Let's talk about the POC shape: we want to run a 72-hour benchmark simulating our bursty traffic, with one scenario for hosted and another for Dedicated.
[07:59] Liam Patel: Sounds good. Sofia — can you propose the exact pool size and test parameters?
[08:03] Sofia Martinez: For 2k TPS bursts with 200ms avg generation we recommend a 5 to 8 GPU dedicated pool with burst reserve. We'll propose three test phases: baseline at 200 TPS, burst test at 2k TPS for 30-90s windows, and a long-context run with 150k tokens per session.
[08:20] Priya Shah: For the long-context run we need to ensure tokenization parity; does Redwood use the same tokenizer as our prod models?
[08:26] Harper Nguyen: We expose tokenizer details and can run tokenizer parity checks; if there's a mismatch we can compile a compatible model variant.
[08:33] Jordan Lee: About failures and SLOs — what SLA do you offer for Dedicated?
[08:38] Liam Patel: Dedicated has an SLA with latency and uptime targets and penalty credits. We'll share the SLA doc.
[08:44] Ethan Park: If a model variant changes through an automated rollout, is there an automatic rollback?
[08:49] Sofia Martinez: Yes, rollouts have built-in health checks: error rate, latency, and quality regression on a small eval set. If thresholds exceeded we auto rollback.
[08:58] Jordan Lee: Any gotchas with resumable streams across model variants?
[09:03] Harper Nguyen: The main gotcha is tokenizer/kv layout differences in quantized variants — resume tokens include compatibility metadata and the Console will mark incompatible variants.
[09:15] Liam Patel: (shifts tone) We'll now show a scripted failure: hit OOM on GPU, then see what the client sees when reconnecting.
[09:23] Sofia Martinez: (sim) OOM triggered, runtime drains, routing shifts, and clients get resume tokens. Watch the client side — reconnect, pass resume token, continue.
[09:38] Maya Ortiz: I see a short gap then the stream continued, that's acceptable.
[09:42] Priya Shah: For audit workloads we can't afford summarization; we'd prefer dedicated with more RAM and to persist raw token streams — can Redwood persist tokens to our S3?
[09:51] Harper Nguyen: Yes, we can forward raw token streams or transcripts to customer-controlled S3 buckets; encryption with your KMS is supported.
[09:59] Jordan Lee: Ok, two more product questions: 1) How does Optimize recommend batching without adding latency? 2) How do you measure quality regressions for quantization across our prompt set?
[10:10] Sofia Martinez: Optimize analyzes request shape and suggests batching windows that maximize GPU utilization within your latency SLO. For quality, we run your eval set through candidate quantized models and measure deltas in generated metrics and task-specific evals; results are in the Console so you can decide tradeoffs.
[10:27] Liam Patel: (wrap) To recap — we'll send pricing and the private deployment checklist, schedule the POC for next week pending your traffic traces, and share the security docs. Any final questions?
[10:39] Jordan Lee: Timeline — we need POC results and an internal decision by end of month. Will you be able to turn around the benchmark quickly?
[10:45] Sofia Martinez: Yes, once we have traces and sample prompts we'll spin up the test harness; initial results usually within 72-96 hours.
[10:52] Harper Nguyen: I'll also add initial optimization recommendations in a short doc.
[10:56] Jordan Lee: Great, thanks everyone.
[10:58] Liam Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the action items.
[11:02] (call ends)

Notes about transcription quality: occasional mis-hearings around kernel names and acronyms (e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-Vcash), minor speaker attribution errors.
